title: Liouvillian Response for Temporal Information in Quantum Reservoir Computing
authors: Jiande Cao, Rui-Yang Gong, Zhongjin Lin, Yexiong Zeng, Ze-Liang Xiang
abstract: Open quantum systems offer a physical substrate for temporal information processing in quantum reservoir computing, yet the microscopic mechanisms linking their dynamics to computational performance remain unclear. Here we establish a microscopic response-to-performance framework that connects Liouvillian dynamics directly to task performance. We decompose observable Volterra weights as $W^{(q)}=BH^{(q)}$, separating internal input-history pathways from their readout visibility, and show that a dynamical response contributes to a task only if it is input-generated, readout-visible, target-correlated, and resolvable above the regularization scale. This framework reveals how Liouvillian modes govern the retention and propagation of task-relevant information, while symmetries determine which components remain visible to the readout. It further establishes how distinct covariance modes encode different temporal information structures and how system parameters and processing protocols can reshape their contributions to improve QRC performance. Thermalization drives the reservoir from processing that retains input history to a response dominated by the most recent input before regularization suppresses the residual information. We finally show that weak measurement can activate task-relevant covariance modes by lifting symmetry-imposed channel equivalence, whereas delayed feedback creates controlled return pathways for historical information. These results establish a microscopic connection between open-system dynamics and computational performance, providing principles for engineering task-relevant information flow in quantum reservoirs.
summary: This paper develops a rigorous, microscopic framework to link the dynamics of open quantum systems to their performance in Quantum Reservoir Computing. By decomposing system weights and analyzing the role of Liouvillian modes, the authors show that computational success depends on specific, measurable properties of the system's information flow. The results provide actionable principles for engineering quantum reservoirs using techniques like weak measurement and feedback control.
main_problem: To establish a microscopic framework connecting the open-system dynamics (Liouvillian evolution) of quantum reservoirs to their actual computational performance in Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC).
main_result: The framework shows that useful dynamic responses must be input-generated, readout-visible, target-correlated, and resolvable. Furthermore, weak measurement and delayed feedback can actively control and enhance the flow of task-relevant historical information.
method: The authors develop a microscopic response-to-performance framework by decomposing Volterra weights and analyzing the system's evolution under Liouvillian dynamics, incorporating techniques for open-loop and closed-loop weight calculation.
model_or_system: The study uses open quantum systems as reservoirs, modeled by Liouvillian dynamics. Specific physical realizations include interacting Ising spin systems and multipoint-coupled waveguide QED systems, all driven by external inputs.
key_observables: Liouvillian modes, covariance modes, Volterra weights ($W^{(q)}$), NRMSE, and Memory Capacity (MC).
important_parameters: Regularization scale, feedback parameter ($ eta$), and the structure of the input drive ($s_n$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on approximations such as the Markov approximation for the waveguide and assumes that the classical feedback loop preserves the structure of the readout projection.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the general framework connecting Liouvillian dynamics to performance. It then details the application to specific physical models (Ising, QED), deriving the mathematical tools for open-loop and closed-loop weight calculations, and finally analyzing how feedback and measurement modify the weight structure to improve task performance.
why_interesting: This work provides deep, quantitative insights into how the underlying physics of open quantum systems dictates their utility as computational substrates, offering concrete engineering principles for quantum information processing.
